# dsh-codex-bridge
Observe and steer a local **Codex** (OpenAI) session from **DeepSeek Harness**.

The plugin talks to `codex app-server` — the same protocol the Codex app itself
uses — which is what
makes the live parts possible at all:
| | Reading the rollout `.jsonl` | This plugin |

| Transcript | after it is written | live deltas, plus polls |
| Reasoning | only what was flushed |

summary deltas as they stream |
| Rate-limit budget | not present | `account/rateLimits/read` |
| S

end a message | not possible | queue (the only cross-process path) |
| Answer an approval | not poss
ible | only for turns this bridge started |

It was built as a DSH counterpart to a Codex session running in the Codex desktop
app: read what tha

t session is doing, hand it the next instruction, and know
exactly which parts are impossible rather

ing, hand it the next instruction, and know
exactly which parts are impossible rather than guessing.
## Tools
| Tool | What it does |
| `codex_status` | Account, plan, rate-limit budget, local processes, latest thread, pending approva

ls. Degrades to a readable message when Codex is not reachable instead of throwing. |
| `codex_threa

ds` | Recent threads, optionally filtered by a search string. |
| `codex_transcript` | Items of one

thread, newest first. |
| `codex_watch` | Watches a thread for N seconds and returns what streamed p
ast, merging the live notification stream with transcript polls and labelling each event's `source`.

|
| `codex_send` | `queue` (default), `turn`, or `steer`. Falls back to the queue when the desktop

app holds the thread's write lock. |
[该节后续省略]
### What it sends

Not a bare "continue". Every automatic message is a **supervision brief** built from
that thread's o

wn record — and only from it: the goal objective Codex was given,
Codex's own last `agentMessage` wo

rd for word (with its phase), the newest turn's
status and, when it failed, the error text Codex rec

orded plus how long ago that was,
the item counts for the turn, and whether a queue is still unconsu

med. Nothing is
paraphrased and nothing is invented; where the record is empty the brief says so
(`这
个线程没有记录目标`, `没有留下可读的回复文字`).
### What it will and will not pick up

A red thread stays red when a person really is needed. The failure is classified from
Codex's own er
ror text, and only two kinds are retried:

- **retryable** — `transient` (dropped stream, transport/network error, 502/503/504,
timeout) and `c

ontext` (context window exhausted). These are runs that stopped
mid-flight, not decisions, so the br

ief says `这类失败可以直接重试，不必等人`.
- **never retried** — `quota` (usage limit, rate limit, spend control),

`auth`
(credentials, 401/403), and `unknown`, which is anything the pattern list does not
recognise.
The brief then says not to retry and to state what it needs instead.

A thread waiting on an approval, a turn that asked a question, a queue that is not
empty, a turn tha

t moved less than 90 seconds ago, the same stuck turn twice, or the
per-thread and per-run caps all

still stop it. Two failed sends halt that thread
and the strip says so, and a thread paused by hand

is skipped and shows an
`autopilot paused here` chip. Arming expires on its own after 30 minutes, `S

top keeping it
moving` ends it immediately, and every decision — sent, skipped, halted, with the
mes

sage it sent, quoted in full — is listed in the strip. Cards that failed carry a
`retryable failure

(transient)` / `needs a person (quota)` line quoting the error, so
what the supervisor decided and w

hy is visible on the card, not just in the log. It
never answers an approval: a person still does th

is visible on the card, not just in the log. It
never answers an approval: a person still does that.

The classification is pattern matching over Codex's own error strings — a heuristic,
not a diagnosis

, and the module says so in every string it produces. It is written to
fail closed: an unrecognised
failure is left for a person rather than retried blindly.

The client half is plain JS loaded by the web client — no build step, like the
shipped client plugin

s, and it is re-read from disk on page load. The host half is
imported at startup, so host changes n
eed a Harness restart.
## What you cannot do, and why

Five of these are **structural**, not missing features — full evidence in
`docs/limitations.md`:

1. **The desktop app holds an exclusive write lock on every thread it has opened**,
even while idle.

So `turn`/`steer` are unavailable for those threads and
`queue` is the only write path.
2. **Approv

als go to the client that owns the turn.** For a turn the Codex app is
running, `codex_approvals` se

es nothing and cannot answer for it. Approving the
app's turns from here is impossible over this pro

tocol.
3. **Live deltas go only to the owning connection.** Watching a desktop-owned
thread works, b

ut through polling, so it is up to ~1.2s behind and arrives as
`source: "transcript"`.
4. **Reasonin

g bodies are encrypted.** You get the emitted summary — rendered as
`(reasoning not exposed: encrypt

ed)` when there is none — not the hidden chain
of thought.
5. **This plugin cannot push into a Harne

ss conversation.** There is no protocol
method to hand a Codex thread's state to another process, an

d the panel is
called by the page, not the other way round. A takeover is therefore prepared
for a p

erson (or a later Harness turn, via `codex_handoff action=claim`), never
injected.

Also: `codex_send` is a **real write**, and the board's autopilot is a second, much
narrower one (qu

eue only, armed by a click, capped, expiring, and logged). A queued
message is picked up promptly —

in testing, almost immediately — so queueing is
sending, not drafting.
`codex_queue action=delete` c

an cancel an entry that is still waiting, but that is
a race rather than an undo: the tool reports t

he app-server's own answer instead of
assuming the message never went out.

- Node >= 22 (uses `node:test`, ESM, `randomUUID`)
- A Codex install for anything live; the unit tes
